The 'shine as the lights of heaven' echoes Daniel 12:3 ('they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament') and anticipates Matthew 13:43 ('Then shall the righteous shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father'). Tewahedo eschatology preserves this glorification-by-shining as the proper image of the resurrection body: not pale ghost, not generic light, but glorified material radiance that is recognizably the individual person now made luminous.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 104:2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD. Cf. Dan 12:3 + Mt 13:43.

entries.summary: 'The Holy Great One will come forth from His dwelling, and the eternal God will tread upon the earth, even on Mount Sinai, and appear in the strength of His might from the heaven of heavens' — the Sinai theophany extended to a general theological pattern. The God who once came down on Sinai will come again at the eschaton; the historical theophany prefigures the eschatological. The Tewahedo Synaxarium readings for the Feast of the Transfiguration explicitly connect this verse to the Tabor manifestation: each visible coming of the Most High to creation participates in the one cosmic visitation that the Mäṣḥafä Hēnok foretells.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 1:3-4, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'Observe ye everything that takes place in the heaven, how they do not change their orbits, and the luminaries which are in the heaven, how they all rise and set in order, each in its season, and transgress not against their appointed order' — the natural-theology argument from cosmic regularity. The Watchers' rebellion is precisely the violation of this divinely-appointed cosmic order; the natural creation's obedience shames the angelic-human disobedience. The Tewahedo monastic tradition draws explicit catechetical use: the unfailing observance of natural creation rebukes the failing observance of moral creation.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 2:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'But ye — ye have not been steadfast, nor done the commandments of the Lord' — the address to the unrighteous after the natural-theology argument of chs 2-5. The transgression is specifically of the COMMANDMENTS, not of vague moral sensibility: 1 Enoch presupposes the Mosaic covenant as the standard by which the elect are measured. The Tewahedo reading takes this as the canonical Jewish covenant-theology basis that the Christian moral catechesis presupposes; the Sermon on the Mount intensifies but does not abrogate the prior commanded standard.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 5:4, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'But to the elect there shall be light and joy and peace, and they shall inherit the earth' — the climactic blessing on the righteous, anticipating the Beatitude 'Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth' (Mt 5:5 = Ps 37:11). The triple gift (light + joy + peace) Tewahedo eschatology reads as the proper inheritance of the resurrection saints: not merely escape from suffering but positive participation in divine glory. The 'inherit the earth' is read in Tewahedo eschatology as the new-creation earth, restored and glorified, not the present fallen earth.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 5:7, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD. Cf. Mt 5:5 + Ps 37:11.

entries.summary: 'And the angels, the children of the heaven, saw and lusted after them, and said to one another: Come, let us choose us wives from among the children of men and beget us children' — the deliberate-collective character of the Watchers' decision. The rebellion is not impulsive individual passion but coordinated council: 'said to one another' frames the sin as conspiratorial, not accidental. The Tewahedo angelological tradition reads this against any reading that would minimize Satan-and-the-fallen-angels as mere temptation-creatures: they are genuine moral agents with developed plans, not impulsive nature-spirits.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 6:2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'Then sware they all together and bound themselves by mutual imprecations upon it' — the angelic oath that seals the rebellion. The mutual binding-by-oath ensures no individual angel can retreat from the collective plan: each is now bound to all the others. Tewahedo demonological tradition reads this as the prototype of every subsequent secret-society oath: the binding-by-mutual-imprecation is the demonic technology for ensuring collective evil endures past individual second-thoughts. The verse warrants a deep ascetic suspicion of any oath-bound association outside the Church's sacramental order.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 6:5, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'The giants turned against them and devoured mankind. And they began to sin against birds, and beasts, and reptiles, and fish, and to devour one another's flesh, and drink the blood' — the violent escalation of giant predation. The four-fold catalog (humans / birds / beasts / fish) traces the giant predation through the whole creaturely order; 'devour one another's flesh' makes them ultimately self-cannibalistic. Tewahedo monastic-ascetic tradition reads this as the ultimate pattern of disordered appetite: unchecked consumption finally turns inward, devouring its own. The catalog itself becomes the textual basis for the standard four-fold dietary categories preserved in monastic fasting rules.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 7:5-6, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And as men perished, they cried, and their cry went up to heaven' — the foundational text for the prayer-of-the-oppressed as cosmic-judicial appeal. The 'cry' (Geez 'awyāt) is involuntary lament of those suffering injustice; it ascends to heaven by divine ordinance, not by deliberate liturgical mediation. This is the textual basis for the Tewahedo doctrine of God's predisposition to hear the cry of the persecuted regardless of formal liturgical observance: oppression itself becomes prayer when borne by the innocent.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 8:4, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'Then Michael, Uriel, Raphael, and Gabriel looked down from heaven and saw much blood being shed upon the earth' — the four-archangel intercession that responds to the cry of the oppressed. The four names establish the canonical Tewahedo angelology: Michael (warrior-defender), Uriel (light-bearer / scribe), Raphael (healer / binder of Azazel), Gabriel (messenger). Other Christian traditions know one or two of these; the Tewahedo Synaxarium honors all four with dedicated feast days, drawing the angelological framework directly from this Enochic chapter.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 9:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: The archangels address the Most High: 'Lord of lords, God of gods, King of kings, and God of the ages, the throne of Thy glory standeth unto all the generations of the ages, and Thy name holy and glorious and blessed unto all the ages' — the foundational angelic doxology. The triple superlative (Lord of lords + God of gods + King of kings) becomes the Tewahedo liturgical model for naming God in the Anaphora prayers; 'King of kings' specifically (mèngèshte negus) becomes the Ethiopian imperial title (Negus Negesti = King of Kings) borrowed from this verse. The Tewahedo Anaphora of the Apostles preserves this Enochic doxology pattern verbatim.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 9:4, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And they have gone to the daughters of men upon the earth, and have slept with the women, and have defiled themselves' — the archangels' formal indictment of the Watchers. The verb 'defiled themselves' (Geez 'irat) Tewahedo reads not merely as ritual impurity but as ontological self-degradation: the Watchers' descent into human sexuality reduces their angelic substance to a corrupted mixed-state. This grounds the Tewahedo monastic-ascetic theology of celibacy: not because sexuality is evil (Gen 1:28 stands) but because angelic-ranked existence has always been celibate by nature, and the monastic call is to anticipate that angelic mode of life.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 9:8, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'Then said the Most High, the Holy and Great One spake, and sent Uriel to the son of Lamech' — God's first response to the angelic intercession: dispatching Uriel to Noah. The naming of Noah as 'son of Lamech' (rather than directly) establishes the genealogical-historical anchoring of the divine intervention: God acts within recognizable human history, working through specific named individuals embedded in known lineages. Tewahedo theological reading takes this as the Enochic anchor for the doctrine of providence working through ordinary genealogical paths rather than through general moral suasion.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 10:1-2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: Of the rebel Watchers: 'In those days they shall be led off to the abyss of fire, and to the torment and the prison in which they shall be confined for ever' — the final-judgment confinement of the rebel angels. The 'abyss of fire' (Geez gehannem) is etymologically the Geez form of Gehenna; this is the textual root of Tewahedo eschatology's specifically-fiery doctrine of the fate of the unrepentant. 'For ever' (la-'alam — for the age, into the eternal) precludes any annihilationist reading: the punishment is eternal in duration, matching the eternal-good reward of the elect.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 10:13, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in those days I will open the store chambers of blessing which are in the heaven, so as to send them down upon the earth over the work and labour of the children of men' — the eschatological reversal of the Watcher-era curse. Where the Watchers brought down forbidden teachings + ruinous consequences, the Most High at the eschaton will open the legitimate heavenly storehouses + send down the blessings on human labor. The 'work and labour of the children of men' is restored to its Edenic dignity by divine cooperation rather than usurped by demonic technological revelation.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 11:1-2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'Before these things Enoch was hidden, and no one of the children of men knew where he was hidden, and where he abode, and what had become of him' — the foundational text for Enoch's hidden pre-translation existence. Already before the Flood narrative, Enoch is 'hidden' (Geez xəbu') with the watchers and holy ones — translated from ordinary human existence into the angelic order. This Tewahedo reads as the foundation of Enoch's authority to receive subsequent visions: he is the human-yet-translated witness, qualified to mediate between angelic and human knowledge precisely because he occupies both spheres.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 12:1-2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: The angels commission Enoch: 'Enoch, thou scribe of righteousness, go, declare to the Watchers of the heaven who have left the high heaven, the holy eternal place, and have defiled themselves with women' — Enoch's prophetic-judicial role as scribe. Where ordinary scribes record human events, Enoch is the scribe of the angelic-judicial process: the divine sentence on the Watchers passes THROUGH Enoch's recording. The title 'scribe of righteousness' (ṣaḥafe ṣədq) becomes the canonical Tewahedo designation; this verse is the textual warrant for treating Enoch's recorded visions as inspired prophetic Scripture rather than mere human composition.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 12:4, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: The fallen Watchers ask Enoch to intercede for them: 'They had not the power to speak with Him or to lift up their eyes to heaven for shame of their sins for which they had been condemned' — the inability of the fallen to face God directly. The shame-condition Tewahedo reads as the inverse of the elect's privileged direct address to God (cf. Heb 4:16 'come boldly unto the throne of grace'): unrepented sin produces moral inability to approach, even apart from any external prohibition. The Tewahedo confessional-sacramental theology reads this as the textual basis for the priest's mediating role in sin-burdened conscience.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 13:5, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: After Enoch's attempted intercession, the divine response: 'And the vision was shown to me thus: Behold, in the vision clouds invited me and a mist summoned me' — the prelude to God's denial of forgiveness for the fallen Watchers. The denial itself comes in chs 14-16: the Watchers' rebellion is not forgivable because they sinned with full angelic knowledge, where humans sin with partial knowledge. Tewahedo theological tradition draws explicit distinction: human sin is fully redeemable through Christ's incarnation (the Word assumed human nature); angelic sin is not (the Word did not assume angelic nature). The Mäṣḥafä Hēnok grounds this distinction textually.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 13:8, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'The book of the words of righteousness, and of the reprimand of the eternal Watchers in accordance with the command of the Holy Great One in that vision' — the literary-canonical self-description of the section that follows. The text identifies itself as 'the book' (mäṣḥaf) of the words of righteousness — claiming for itself the canonical-scriptural status that the Tewahedo tradition recognizes. The naming of God as 'the Holy Great One' (Qadūs ʿAbiy) becomes a standard Tewahedo liturgical title, preserved in the Anaphora.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 14:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: Of the Most High in the throne vision: 'No angel could enter and could behold His face by reason of the magnificence and glory, and no flesh could behold Him' — the divine inaccessibility even to the highest angels. The 'no angel could enter' establishes the radical otherness of God even from the angelic order: God is not merely the highest among the heavenly hierarchy but qualitatively other than the entire creaturely order, including angels. This grounds the Tewahedo apophatic theological tradition: divine essence is incomprehensible to every creature, including the highest cherubim and seraphim.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 14:25, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: Of the giants born from the Watcher-human unions: 'But now the giants, who are produced from the spirits and flesh, shall be called evil spirits upon the earth, and on the earth shall be their dwelling' — the foundational Enochic etiology of demons. The giants (Nephilim) die in the Flood; their disembodied spirits become the unclean spirits that the New Testament accounts will exorcise. This is the Tewahedo demonological tradition's textual root: demons are not eternally-fallen lower angels but specifically the disembodied spirits of the antediluvian giants. The exorcistic ministry of Christ (cf. Mk 1:23-27 + parallels) presupposes this Enochic understanding.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 15:8-10, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD. Cf. Mk 1:23-27.

entries.summary: Of the demons (disembodied giants): 'From the day of the slaughter and destruction and death of the giants, from the souls of whose flesh the spirits, having gone forth, shall destroy without incurring judgement' — the post-Flood era of demonic predation. The demons act 'without incurring judgement' because they exist in a category outside the original divine ordering: humans face judgment under the Adamic-Noahic-Mosaic covenant; angels face judgment for their own rebellion; demons (as a third category, post-Flood) operate in an interim awaiting final eschatological judgment. The Tewahedo exorcistic liturgical tradition draws explicit pneumatological framework from this verse.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 16:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And they took and brought me to a place in which those who were there were like flaming fire, and, when they wished, they appeared as men' — the opening of Enoch's first cosmic journey. The angelic guides who transform between fire-form and man-form establish the Enochic angelological pattern: angels have native fire-existence (their proper-nature mode) but can manifest as men for human communication (their accommodation-mode). The Tewahedo iconographic tradition preserves this dual-mode angelology: angels are depicted in human form in iconographic accommodation, but liturgical-theological references invoke their fire-nature.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 17:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And I came to the river of fire in which the fire flows like water and discharges itself into the great sea towards the west' — Enoch beholds the river of fire that connects to the cosmic west-sea. The river-of-fire (nahar ʾəsāt) Tewahedo eschatology reads as the eschatological fire that purges + judges; the New Testament's 'lake of fire' (Rev 19:20, 20:10) Tewahedo reads as connected to this Enochic vision. The 'great sea towards the west' is the cosmic-mythic ocean at the world's edge, before which the fire-river ends — establishing the geographical-eschatological boundary of the divine economy.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 17:5, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD. Cf. Rev 19:20.

entries.summary: The angel-guide tells Enoch: 'This place is the end of heaven and earth: this has become a prison for the stars and the host of heaven' — the prison of the fallen stars. The 'stars' here are angelic beings (per ancient Near Eastern cosmology where stars are the visible counterparts of heavenly powers); the prison is where the Watcher-stars who transgressed are confined awaiting judgment. Jude 1:13's 'wandering stars, to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever' Tewahedo reads as direct allusion to this Enochic verse. The cosmology of stars-as-angels is preserved in Tewahedo liturgical hymnody.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 18:14, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD. Cf. Jude 1:13.

entries.summary: Uriel explains: 'Here shall stand the angels who have connected themselves with women, and their spirits assuming many different forms are defiling mankind and shall lead them astray into sacrificing to demons as gods' — the post-Flood human idolatry derived from demon-led seduction. Tewahedo reads this as the canonical-Jewish anchor for the New Testament's claim that pagan sacrifices are sacrifices 'to demons' (1 Cor 10:20: 'the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils, and not to God'). The continuity between 1 Enoch's demonology and Paul's pagan-idolatry critique is one of the strongest inter-textual bridges the Tewahedo canon preserves.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 19:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD. Cf. 1 Cor 10:20.

entries.summary: Enoch concludes his vision report: 'And I, Enoch, alone saw the vision, the ends of all things: and no man shall see as I have seen' — the Enochic claim to unique revelatory privilege. The 'no man shall see' establishes Enoch's prophetic singularity (until the eschaton's general revelation). Tewahedo reads this not as exclusivist boast but as commissioned-witness charter: Enoch sees so that he may report, his vision is recorded so that the elect may know what they could not otherwise know. The verse becomes the textual warrant for the Mäṣḥafä Hēnok's canonical-scriptural status: the unique vision requires preservation in inspired text.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 19:3, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And these are the names of the holy angels who watch' — the foundational seven-archangel list: Uriel (chief of the host of the firmament + chief of paradise + chief of the cherubim), Raphael (chief of the spirits of men), Raguel (over the world of the luminaries), Michael (chief of Israel + over chaos), Saraqael (the spirits of the children of men who transgress), Gabriel (over paradise + serpents + cherubim), Remiel (over those who rise from the dead). The Tewahedo Synaxarium honors all seven on dedicated days; the seven-archangel framework is one of the most explicit Tewahedo angelological inheritances from the Mäṣḥafä Hēnok, with Catholic and Orthodox traditions partially preserving the framework but Protestant traditions almost entirely losing it.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 20:1-7, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And from thence I went to another place, which was still more horrible than the former, and I saw a horrible thing: a great fire there which burnt and blazed, and the place was cleft as far as the abyss, being full of great descending columns of fire' — the Tartaros-Gehenna vision. Enoch sees the place of final punishment for the wicked, distinguished from the prison of the rebel angels in 18:14 by its more-horrible character. The fire descending in columns Tewahedo reads as the inverse of the Pentecostal tongues of fire descending in blessing (Acts 2:3): the same fire-imagery serves either as gift (when received by the righteous Spirit) or as judgment (when meeting the unrighteous).
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 21:7, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD. Cf. Acts 2:3.

entries.summary: 'And from thence I went to another place to the west of the ends of the earth. And I saw a burning fire which ran without resting, and paused not from its course day or night but ran regularly' — Enoch beholds the perpetual fire of the divine judicial process. The 'without resting' (Geez 'enza i-yenuh) establishes the perpetuity of divine judgment: the fire of judgment is not episodic but ongoing, constantly burning even when not visibly applied. This grounds the Tewahedo theological reading that divine justice is not occasional intervention but continuous operation — what humans experience as discrete acts of judgment are visible occasions of a permanently-burning process.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 23:1-2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And amongst them was a tree such as I had never yet smelt, neither was any amongst them nor were others like it: it had a fragrance beyond all fragrance, and its leaves and blooms and wood wither not for ever: and its fruit is beautiful' — Enoch's vision of the eschatological tree of life. The tree restored at the eschaton echoes the Edenic tree (Gen 2:9) and prefigures the Revelation tree of life (Rev 22:2 'the tree of life, which bare twelve manner of fruits, and yielded her fruit every month: and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations'). Tewahedo eschatology preserves the tree-of-life imagery as central to its description of the restored creation; the Mäṣḥafä Hēnok's vision pre-dates and grounds the Revelation development.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 24:4, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD. Cf. Rev 22:2.

entries.summary: The angel Michael explains the mountain on which the tree of life grows: 'This high mountain which thou hast seen, whose summit is like the throne of God, is His throne, where the Holy Great One, the Lord of Glory, the Eternal King, will sit, when He shall come down to visit the earth with goodness' — the throne-mountain of the eschatological visitation. The mountain serves simultaneously as God's throne AND as the place of His descent to creation: in the eschaton the transcendent and immanent are reunited geographically. Tewahedo theological geography preserves this throne-mountain imagery; Mount Zion (and by extension every consecrated church building) participates in this eschatological throne-mountain typology.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 25:3, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: Of the tree of life at the eschaton: 'Its fruit shall be for food to the elect: it shall be transplanted to the holy place, to the temple of the Lord, the Eternal King' — the transplantation of the tree to the eschatological temple. The tree of life is not merely restored to its Edenic location but UPGRADED to the temple of God Himself: the original garden setting becomes the new-creation sanctuary. Tewahedo liturgical theology reads this as the textual basis for the consecrated altar table as participation in the eschatological temple-tree: the eucharistic bread received at the altar IS the fruit of the eschatological tree of life given proleptically.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 25:5, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And I went from thence to the middle of the earth, and I saw a blessed place in which there were trees with branches abiding and blooming. And there I saw a holy mountain, and underneath the mountain to the east there was a stream and it flowed towards the south' — Enoch beholds the cosmic-geographical center of the earth: Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives. The middle-of-the-earth cosmology (with Jerusalem at the omphalos / world's navel) Tewahedo preserves in its theological geography; the medieval mappae mundi place Jerusalem at the center because of this Enochic-and-prophetic tradition.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 26:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: The angel explains the cursed Valley of Hinnom: 'This accursed valley is for those who are accursed for ever: here shall all the accursed be gathered together who utter with their lips against the Lord unseemly words and of His glory speak hard things' — the Gehenna eschatology grounded in geographical Hinnom Valley outside Jerusalem. The valley where idolatrous Israel sacrificed children to Molech becomes the Mäṣḥafä Hēnok's typological location of the eschatological gathering of the condemned. New Testament 'Gehenna' (12 occurrences) presupposes this Enochic geographical-eschatological identification; Tewahedo eschatology preserves the Hinnom-Gehenna typological continuity.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 27:2-3, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And I saw the trees of judgement, especially vessels of the fragrance of frankincense and myrrh, and the trees were not like each other' — Enoch's vision of the aromatic trees of paradise: frankincense and myrrh prominent among them. The same two substances are brought as gifts to the infant Christ (Mt 2:11) — Tewahedo Christological reading takes the Magi gifts as proleptic offering from the eschatological paradise back to the Incarnate one whose advent inaugurates the new creation. The Tewahedo eucharistic preparation includes frankincense + myrrh in deliberate liturgical-cosmic reference.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 29:2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD. Cf. Mt 2:11.

entries.summary: 'And I came to the Garden of Righteousness, and saw beyond those trees many large trees growing there and of goodly fragrance, large, very beautiful and glorious, and the tree of wisdom whereof they eat and know great wisdom' — Enoch reaches the Edenic Garden of Righteousness with the tree of wisdom (distinct from the tree of life at 24:4 and 25:5). The Garden of Righteousness as the proper-name designation of restored Eden becomes determinative for Tewahedo monastic-spiritual literature: the monastery is figured as the proleptic Garden of Righteousness on earth, where the tree of wisdom yields its fruit to the disciplined ascetic.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 32:3, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And there I saw the ends of the earth whereon the heaven rests, and the portals of the heaven open. And I saw how the stars of heaven come forth, and I counted the portals out of which they proceed' — Enoch's vision of the cosmological mechanism by which stars rise and set. The 'portals' (Geez bāʾəw) are gates in the heavenly dome through which the heavenly bodies pass on their appointed circuits. Tewahedo theological cosmology preserves this gateway-cosmology in its liturgical hymnody: the doxologies frequently reference the 'portals of heaven' through which prayers ascend and divine gifts descend.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 33:3, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And from thence I went towards the north to the ends of the earth, and there I saw a great and glorious device at the ends of the whole earth' — Enoch's northward journey reaches the cosmic north device. The 'great and glorious device' (Geez maxbar 'abiy wa-səbuh) Tewahedo cosmological tradition reads as the divine mechanism for weather: the storehouses of snow, rain, and wind from which the meteorological phenomena are dispatched per divine will. This pre-meteorological cosmology Tewahedo monasticism preserves as catechetical resource: weather is not merely natural but divinely-administered, and prayer for rain is real petition to the administering Most High.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 34:1-3, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And from thence I went to the south to the ends of the earth, and saw there three open portals of the heaven: from them issues dew, rain, and wind' — Enoch's final journey-segment to the south completes the four-directional cosmological survey (chs 17-36). Together with the earlier western (17-19) and northern (34) journeys + the central Jerusalem-omphalos vision (26-32), Enoch has now mapped the cosmic geography from all four cardinal directions. The Tewahedo iconographic tradition's depictions of the cosmos often preserve this four-directional structuring with Jerusalem at the center, drawing on the Enochic cosmological survey as authoritative source.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 36:1-4, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'Until the present day such wisdom has never been given by the Lord of Spirits as I have received... that I should declare it to those who dwell on the earth' — Enoch's commissioning to deliver the Parables not as private mysticism but as covenant proclamation. The Tewahedo Synaxarium retains Enoch's prophetic status as one to whom the heavenly wisdom-tradition was entrusted, the textual basis for the liturgical reading of 1 Enoch in select Tewahedo festal contexts.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 37:5, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'When the Righteous One shall appear before the eyes of the righteous, whose elect works hang upon the Lord of Spirits, and light shall appear to the righteous and the elect who dwell on the earth' — first occurrence of 'the Righteous One' (Ge'ez ṣadiq) as an eschatological title. Tewahedo Christology reads this title prospectively as a designation for Christ, paralleling Acts 3:14, 7:52, 22:14 — the New Testament's ho dikaios as Christological title shares the Enochic verbal root.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 38:2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'From thenceforward those who possess the earth shall no longer be powerful and exalted: nor shall they be able to behold the face of the holy, for the Lord of Spirits has caused His light to appear on the face of the holy and righteous and elect' — reversal of social ordering at the eschaton. Tewahedo wisdom tradition reads this verse as parallel to the Magnificat (Lk 1:51-53): both preserve the prophetic God-shines-on-the-humble / God-throws-down-the-mighty structure under Lord-of-Spirits theology.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 38:4, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And there mine eyes saw the Elect One of righteousness and of faith, and I saw his dwelling-place under the wings of the Lord of Spirits' — the Elect One pre-existent and enthroned-with-the-Father. Tewahedo iconography of Christ enthroned under the wings of the Lord (preserved in some illuminated Ge'ez Bibles' depictions of the throne-room visions) traces back to this verse as scriptural anchor for the imagery.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 39:6, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And those who sleep not bless Thee: they stand before Thy glory and bless, praise, and extol, saying: "Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord of Spirits: he filleth the earth with spirits"' — the triple-sanctus (qadis qadis qadis) attested in the Parables. The Tewahedo Anaphora of the Apostles preserves this Sanctus verbatim as the angelic praise sung perpetually before the throne, drawing both on Isa 6:3 and on the Enochic witness preserved in the Tewahedo lectionary.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 39:12, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And on the four sides of the Lord of Spirits I saw four presences, different from those that sleep not, and I learnt their names: for the angel who went with me made known to me their names' — four-archangel theology of presence (parallel to but distinct from the seven-archangel list at 20:1). Tewahedo iconography of Christ surrounded by the four presences (often depicted on the tabot — the ark's tablets in qǝddǝst, the holy of holies) draws on this verse as canonical authority.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 40:2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the fourth, who is set over the repentance unto hope of those who inherit eternal life, is named Phanuel' — Phanuel as the angel of repentance. Tewahedo penitential tradition retains Phanuel as a distinctive feast-day commemoration (unique to Ethiopia among the major Christian traditions), with his role as the angel-mediator of the sinner's hope preserved in monastic confession liturgy.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 40:9, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And after that I saw all the secrets of the heavens, and how the kingdom is divided, and how the actions of men are weighed in the balance' — the cosmic-balance image. Tewahedo eschatology of judgment as actual weighing (with Michael often depicted as the angel of the scales in church iconography) draws on this verse as scriptural anchor, paralleling Dan 5:27 and standing in lineage with the Egyptian Maat-tradition that Ethiopian iconography preserves through a Christianised filter.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 41:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'For the Lord has separated the day and the night, and the spirits of light and darkness, and apportioned them their seasons' — apportioning theology. Tewahedo wisdom tradition reads this verse in tandem with Gen 1:4-5 as the textual basis for the doctrine that even darkness is ordered toward divine purpose, not autonomous evil — a key node in the Tewahedo theodicy framework.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 41:8, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'Wisdom found no place where she might dwell; then a dwelling-place was assigned her in the heavens. Wisdom went forth to make her dwelling among the children of men, and found no dwelling-place' — the failed earthly mission of Wisdom. Tewahedo Christology reads this verse Christologically (after Pr 8:22-31, Wisd 7:25-26) as anticipating the Incarnation's reversal: the Word/Wisdom who could find no place on earth in the Parables ultimately does find a place — in Mary's womb.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 42:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'Then Wisdom returned to her place, and took her seat among the angels. And iniquity went forth from her chambers: whom she sought not she found, and dwelt with them, as rain in a desert and dew on a thirsty land' — Wisdom's withdrawal contrasted with iniquity's flourishing. Tewahedo monastic qǝne (sacred poetry) preserves this image as the canonical illustration of why Christ's coming was necessary: Wisdom alone could not stay; she required incarnation. The verse is cited in Tewahedo Marian liturgy as the antecedent that Mary's fiat reverses.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 42:2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'These are the names of the holy who dwell on the earth and believe in the name of the Lord of Spirits for ever and ever' — names recorded in heaven for those who believe-in-the-name. Tewahedo baptismal liturgy (in which the catechumen's name is liturgically inscribed and called before the congregation) takes this verse as one of its scriptural anchors, paralleling Lk 10:20 (rejoice that your names are written in heaven).
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 43:4, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'On that day Mine Elect One shall sit on the throne of glory and shall try their works, and their places shall be without number' — the Elect One enthroned for judgment. Tewahedo Christology reads this verse with Mt 25:31 (Son-of-Man on throne-of-glory) as direct textual genealogy: the Synoptic image of the Son of Man enthroned for judgment is verbally Enochic, with the Tewahedo liturgical reading making this dependency explicit.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 45:3, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And I will transform the heaven and make it an eternal blessing and light, and I will transform the earth and make it a blessing: and I will cause Mine elect ones to dwell upon it' — new-heaven-new-earth theology. Tewahedo eschatology reads this verse as parallel and prior textual basis for Rev 21:1-5, with the Parables providing the verbal pattern (transform-heaven-transform-earth) that the Apocalypse expands.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 45:4, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And I asked the angel who went with me and showed me all the hidden things, concerning that Son of Man, who he was, and whence he was, and why he went with the Head of Days' — Enoch's inquiry about the Son of Man, setting up the answer in 46:3. Tewahedo catechesis preserves the question-and-answer dialogical form as the model for inquiring into Christology: the disciple must ASK before the Spirit answers.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 46:2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in those days shall have ascended the prayer of the righteous, and the blood of the righteous from the earth before the Lord of Spirits' — the prayer-of-the-righteous-ascending pattern. Tewahedo intercession theology (the role of saints and martyrs as ongoing intercessors) takes this verse as scriptural foundation for the belief that the martyrs' blood actively cries out before God (parallel to Rev 6:9-10, which draws on this Enochic image).
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 47:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'In those days I saw the Head of Days when He seated himself upon the throne of His glory, and the books of the living were opened before Him: and all His host which is in heaven above and His counsellors stood before Him' — books-of-the-living courtroom scene. The textual genealogy from this image to Dan 7:9-10 to Rev 20:12 forms a continuous Tewahedo eschatological tradition; the books-of-the-living trope appears in the Anaphora of the Three Hundred Eighteen Orthodox.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 47:3, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in that place I saw the fountain of righteousness which was inexhaustible: and around it were many fountains of wisdom: and all the thirsty drank of them, and were filled with wisdom, and their dwellings were with the righteous and holy and elect' — the heavenly fountain. Tewahedo sacramental theology reads this verse as anticipating both baptismal-fountain imagery (the Tewahedo baptismal ritual involves immersion at the church's outer fountain) and the Johannine living-water Christology (Jn 4:14, 7:38).
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 48:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And he shall be a staff to the righteous whereon to stay themselves and not fall, and he shall be the light of the Gentiles, and the hope of those who are troubled of heart' — Light-of-Gentiles title applied to the Son of Man. The verbal parallel to Isa 42:6 / 49:6 (light-to-the-Gentiles) establishes a Servant-of-the-Lord / Son-of-Man identification in pre-Christian Jewish apocalyptic that Tewahedo Christology preserves as canonical: Christ is BOTH suffering-servant AND apocalyptic-Son-of-Man without tension.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 48:4, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the wisdom of the Lord of Spirits hath revealed Him to the holy and righteous; for He hath preserved the lot of the righteous, because they have hated and despised this world of unrighteousness... for in His name they are saved' — the saved-in-his-name formula. Tewahedo soteriology takes this verse as a pre-canonical witness to the in-the-name pattern (Acts 4:12): the Parables already use 'name-of-the-Lord-of-Spirits' as salvation-medium, anticipating the Christological transposition to 'name-of-Jesus' by direct verbal continuity.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 48:7, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'For wisdom is poured out like water, and glory faileth not before him for evermore' — wisdom-as-water. Tewahedo sapiential tradition (qǝne) cites this as the textual basis for the metaphor of teaching as water-pouring; the verse is recited in some Tewahedo monastic chants celebrating the founders' teaching ministry.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 49:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in him dwells the spirit of wisdom, and the spirit which gives insight, and the spirit of understanding and of might, and the spirit of those who have fallen asleep in righteousness' — the multi-spirit-on-the-Messiah list. Strikingly parallel to Isa 11:2's spirit-of-wisdom-and-understanding cluster, and to Rev 5:6's seven-spirits-of-God. Tewahedo pneumatology preserves this triadic resonance (Enoch / Isaiah / Revelation) in the eucharistic epiclesis prayers.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 49:3, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the Elect One shall in those days sit on My throne, and his mouth shall pour forth all the secrets of wisdom and counsel: for the Lord of Spirits hath given them to him and hath glorified him' — Elect-One-on-My-throne. Tewahedo Christology emphasizes the SHARED-throne (Heb 1:3-8; Rev 3:21, 22:1-3) as continuous with this Enochic image: the Son shares the Father's throne not as conquest but as eternal counsel.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 51:3, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'Ye mighty kings who dwell on the earth, ye shall have to behold Mine Elect One, how he sits on the throne of glory and judges Azazel, and all his associates, and all his hosts in the name of the Lord of Spirits' — eschatological judgment of Azazel. Tewahedo demonology reads this verse with 10:13 (Azazel's prior binding) as a two-stage drama: temporal binding (Watchers) plus final eschatological reckoning (Parables) — establishing a pattern that Rev 20:1-10 follows.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 55:4, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the righteous shall be in the light of the sun, and the elect in the light of eternal life: the days of their life shall be unending, and the days of the holy without number' — eternal-light eschatology. Tewahedo eucharistic liturgy invokes this verse imagery in the post-communion prayer 'may we be among those whose days are unending' — direct textual borrowing from the Parables preserved in the Tewahedo liturgical memory.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 58:3, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'In the year 500, in the seventh month, on the fourteenth day of the month in the life of Enoch. In that Parable I saw how a mighty quaking made the heaven of heavens to quake' — opening of the Noah-vision interlude embedded in the Parables. Tewahedo manuscript tradition preserves the Noah-vision as integral to the Parables (some Hellenistic-Jewish witnesses treat it as later interpolation; Ethiopian textual witnesses do not separate it). This editorial decision shapes how Tewahedo readers understand the Parables' coherence.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 60:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And on that day were two monsters parted, a female monster named Leviathan, to dwell in the abysses of the ocean over the fountains of the waters' — Leviathan as cosmic monster. Tewahedo iconographic tradition (preserved on some monastic church murals) retains Leviathan-Behemoth imagery as eschatological-feast preparation, paralleling 2 Bar 29:4, 4 Ezr 6:49-52, b. Sanh 99a — the righteous will eat of these monsters at the Messianic banquet.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 60:7, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the male is named Behemoth, who occupies with his breast a waste wilderness named Dūidāin, on the east of the garden where the elect and righteous dwell' — Behemoth and the Edenic geography. The garden-of-the-righteous remains east-of-Eden, preserving the prelapsarian topology that Tewahedo monastic spirituality maps onto sacred space (the church's qǝddǝst, holy of holies, symbolically corresponds to the inner garden where the righteous dwell).
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 60:8, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the Lord of Spirits placed the Elect One on the throne of glory. And he shall judge all the works of the holy above in the heaven, and in the balance shall their deeds be weighed' — the cosmic-weighing image with the Elect One as judge. Tewahedo iconography of the last judgment (developed especially in the Mäṣḥafä Berhan / Book of Light) depicts Christ as throne-judge with scales held by Michael — drawing on 61:8 as scriptural anchor for the iconographic program.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 61:8, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And he will summon all the host of the heavens, and all the holy ones above, and the host of God, the Cherubic, Seraphin and Ophannin, and all the angels of power' — full angelic hierarchy with the rare Ophannin (= ophanim, the thrones / wheels of Ezk 1:15-21). Tewahedo angelology preserves the threefold-angel structure (Cherubim / Seraphim / Ophanim) in the Sǝbḫata Foṣǝlt prayer, drawing on this verse as canonical authority for naming the third tier.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 61:10, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'In those days shall the mighty and the kings who possess the earth implore (Him) to grant them a little respite from His angels of punishment to whom they were delivered, that they might fall down and worship before the Lord of Spirits, and confess their sins before Him' — the kings' final repentance attempt. Tewahedo homiletic tradition uses this verse to teach that the time of mercy is BEFORE judgment, not after: the kings ask, but 'there shall be no respite' (63:6). The pastoral application is unflinching.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 63:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in those days the punishment of the Lord of Spirits shall go forth, and they shall open all the chambers of waters that are above the heavens, and the springs which are beneath the earth' — cosmic-water-judgment unleashing. Tewahedo eschatological readings (preserved in some Ge'ez liturgical homilies) preserve this water-judgment as parallel to but distinct from the Genesis Flood — eschatological reprise rather than primordial cleansing.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 67:4, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And after that my grandfather Enoch gave me all the secrets in the book of the Parables, and put them together for me in the words of the book of the Parables' — Methuselah as the textual transmitter of the Parables. Tewahedo manuscript culture (the long tradition of monastic scribes copying Enoch) traces its lineage of textual responsibility back through this verse: Methuselah is the first scribe of the Parables, and every Tewahedo scribe stands in that succession.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 68:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the third was named Gadreel: he it is who showed the children of men all the blows of death, and he led astray Eve, and showed the weapons of death to the sons of men, the shield and the coat of mail, and the sword for battle, and all the weapons of death to the children of men' — Gadreel as the angel who taught violence. Tewahedo pacifist-monastic tradition (the demand that monks bear no weapon) cites this verse as the canonical condemnation of weapons-craft at its angelic origin: violence is not natural to creation, it was TAUGHT by a fallen angel.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 69:6, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And by that oath the heaven was suspended before the world was created and for ever. And through it the earth was founded upon the water' — the cosmogonic Oath. Tewahedo wisdom tradition reads this as the textual root for the sacramental power of the divine Name: just as the Oath holds the cosmos together, the invocation of the Name in liturgy holds the worshipping community together. The Sǝbḫata Foṣǝlt invokes this directly.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 69:25, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And he sat on the throne of his glory, and the sum of judgment was given unto the Son of Man, and he caused the sinners to pass away and be destroyed from off the face of the earth, and those who have led the world astray' — Son of Man enthroned at consummation, parallel and prior to Jn 5:22-27. Tewahedo Christology cites this as the textual basis for the doctrine that the Father has GIVEN judgment to the Son — not delegated provisionally, but transferred completely.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 69:27, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And it came to pass after this that his name during his lifetime was raised aloft to that Son of Man and to the Lord of Spirits from amongst those who dwell on the earth' — Enoch's name lifted to the Son of Man, anticipating the climactic 71:14 'Thou art the Son of Man'. Tewahedo theological tradition reads this verse as the textual basis for the unique status accorded Enoch in the Tewahedo Synaxarium: lifted-in-name means lifted-in-priestly-status, with Enoch's intercessory role preserved as part of the heavenly liturgy.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 70:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And he set me between the two winds, between the North and the West, where the angels took the cords to measure for me the place for the elect and righteous' — measuring the place of the righteous. Tewahedo monastic geography (the actual layout of monastic complexes with directional orientation) preserves the four-cardinal-points structuring of sacred space, drawing on 70:3 and parallel Enochic texts as scriptural-cosmological anchor.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 70:3, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the spirit translated Enoch to the heaven of heavens, and I saw there as it were a structure built of crystals, and between those crystals tongues of living fire' — the crystal-and-fire heavenly architecture (parallel to Rev 4:6 sea-of-glass and Rev 21:18-21 crystal city walls). Tewahedo architectural symbolism (the use of polished stone and white-glazed surfaces in Lalibela's monolithic churches) draws on this Enochic vision-architecture as canonical aesthetic.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 71:5, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And I fell on my face, and my whole body became relaxed, and my spirit was transfigured; and I cried with a loud voice... with the spirit of power, and blessed and glorified and extolled' — Enoch's transfiguration. Tewahedo mystical theology reads this verse as a pre-Christian witness to the deification (theosis) tradition: the human person can be transfigured in body and spirit through divine encounter. The Tewahedo monastic feast of Mount Tabor draws explicit liturgical parallels between Christ's Transfiguration and Enoch's, using 71:11 as a reading.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 71:11, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'The first law of the luminaries: the sun has its rising in the eastern portals of the heaven, and its setting in the western portals' — Uriel's revelation of the twelve solar gates governs the entire Enochic calendar system. Tewahedo liturgical computus (Bāḥrä Ḥasab — the 'Sea of Reckoning') preserves a calendar structure that traces ultimately to the Astronomical Book: feast dates are computed by counting from fixed astronomical points rather than from observation, exactly the pattern that 1 Enoch 72 codifies as Uriel's revelation.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 72:2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the year is exactly as to its days three hundred and sixty-four' — the Astronomical Book's 364-day solar calendar (52 weeks exactly, no rollover). The Tewahedo liturgical year follows a 365-day solar pattern in practice (the Coptic-Ethiopian Anno Martyrum calendar), but the 364-day structure of 1 Enoch undergirds the Tewahedo theological insistence that the cosmic year is FIXED and given, not negotiable — a polemic preserved in monastic chronological treatises against later lunisolar adjustments.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 72:32, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And after this law I saw another law dealing with the smaller luminary, which is named the Moon' — moon's law revealed after sun's, establishing the lunar order as derivative and subordinate. Tewahedo cosmology preserves this hierarchical structure (sun-primary, moon-secondary) as theologically significant: just as Christ-the-Sun-of-Righteousness is primary and the Church-as-moon reflects derivative light, the Astronomical Book's ordering of luminaries anticipates the Christological-ecclesiological image preserved in Tewahedo hymnody.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 73:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'Her circumference is like the circumference of the heaven, and her chariot in which she ascends is driven by the wind' — the moon's variable phases governed by wind-driven chariot machinery. Tewahedo monastic natural-philosophy (preserved in the Mashafa Falasfa, the 'Book of the Philosophers') retains this image of celestial bodies as carried by winds — a pre-Aristotelian physics that the Tewahedo tradition preserved while Western scholasticism shifted to the Aristotelian-Ptolemaic crystalline spheres.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 74:2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the leaders of the heads of the thousands, who are placed over the whole creation and over all the stars, have also to do with the four intercalary days, being inseparable from their office' — the intercalary days that complete the calendar's precision. Tewahedo Bāḥrä Ḥasab computation retains the principle of intercalary correction (the 'epact' adjustment) as a fixed angelic ordinance rather than ad-hoc fix: the calendar's accuracy is part of the cosmic priestly liturgy entrusted to the heavenly angelic leaders.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 75:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And on account of them men go wrong therein, for those luminaries truly render service on the world-stations, one in the first portal, one in the third portal of the heaven, and so on' — the polemic against calendar error. Tewahedo liturgical tradition takes this verse seriously as a warning: feast-day timing matters because the cosmic order matters. The Tewahedo Synaxarium's precision on saint-commemoration dates (down to the specific verse of Psalm read on each day) traces theologically to this Enochic concern about getting-the-time-right.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 75:2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And at the ends of the earth I saw twelve portals open to all the regions, from which the winds go forth and blow over the earth' — twelve wind-portals matching the twelve solar gates. Tewahedo iconographic tradition preserves the twelve-wind imagery in some monastic-church frescoes where the cardinal-and-intermediate directions are personified as angelic figures — drawing on the Astronomical Book's catalog of cosmic presences as canonical authority.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 76:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And I saw seven mountains higher than all the mountains which are on the earth: and thence comes forth hoar-frost, and days, seasons, and years pass away. And I saw seven rivers on the earth larger than all the rivers' — sevenfold cosmic geography. Tewahedo monastic geography (the naming of seven holy mountains in Ethiopia, including Debre Damo, Debre Libanos, and the Lalibela complex) preserves the seven-mountains motif as Tewahedo holy-land cosmography, drawing on this Enochic vision.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 77:3, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the names of the sun are the following: the first Orjarēs, and the second Tomāsē. And the moon has four names: the first name is Asōnja, the second Eblā, the third Benāsē, and the fourth Erā' — the named luminaries. Tewahedo angelological tradition preserves the pattern of NAMED celestial beings (rather than impersonal forces): every star has a name known to Uriel and revealed to Enoch, just as every soul has a name known to its guardian angel — the personal-not-impersonal cosmos.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 78:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in the days of the sinners the years shall be shortened, and their seed shall be tardy on their lands and fields, and all things on the earth shall alter, and shall not appear in their time' — sinners' cosmic disruption. Tewahedo eschatological homilies cite this verse as the canonical warning that moral disorder shows up in cosmic disorder — drought, famine, plague — not as punitive intervention but as the natural physical consequence of broken covenant. The verse undergirds Tewahedo fasting-as-restoration theology.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 80:2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And I observed the heavenly tablets, and read everything which was written thereon and understood everything, and read the book of all the deeds of mankind, and of all the children of flesh that shall be upon the earth to the remotest generations' — the heavenly tablets. Tewahedo soteriology preserves the books-of-deeds image (parallel to Rev 20:12) as load-bearing in the Tewahedo last-judgment iconography, with the Enochic version emphasising that the tablets are READABLE — God's record is transparent to inquiry.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 81:2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And now, my son Methuselah, all these things I am recounting to thee and writing down for thee, and I have revealed to thee everything, and given thee books concerning all these: so preserve, my son Methuselah, the books from thy father's hand, and see that thou deliver them to the generations of the world' — the textual transmission charge to Methuselah. Tewahedo monastic-scribal tradition treats this verse as the FOUNDATIONAL warrant for the entire Mäṣḥafä Hēnok preservation enterprise: the Ethiopian scribes who copied Enoch from the 4th century onward stood consciously in this Methuselan succession.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 82:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'I lifted up my hands and prayed and besought and spake, and said: Destroy not the earth; for I have seen the affliction of the earth, and a great destruction. And my grandfather Mahalalel said to me: Wherefore criest thou so, my son?' — Mahalalel's question precedes his interpretation. Tewahedo catechetical tradition preserves the multi-generational form of prophetic transmission preserved here: prophecy is not a private possession but is interpreted across generations within the family-and-tradition that carries it.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 83:7, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And I lifted up my hands in righteousness and blessed the Holy and Great One, and spake with the breath of my mouth, and with the tongue of flesh, which God has made for the children of the flesh of men, that they should speak therewith, and He gave them breath and a tongue and a mouth that they should speak therewith' — the theological warrant for prayer-with-tongue. Tewahedo liturgical theology preserves this as the canonical anchor for the doctrine that human language is GIVEN-for-praise: the tongue's primary purpose is liturgical, not communicative.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 84:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'But now, O God, and Lord and Great King, I implore and beseech Thee to fulfil my prayer, to leave me a posterity on earth, and not destroy all the flesh of man, and make the earth without inhabitant, so that there should be an eternal destruction' — Enoch's intercessory prayer for a righteous remnant. Tewahedo intercessory theology (the saints as ongoing intercessors for the world) reads this prayer as the OT-apocalyptic precedent for the practice — the righteous Enoch interceding for the preservation of any righteous seed at all.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 84:4, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'I saw with mine eyes as I slept, and saw the heaven above, and behold a star fell from heaven, and it arose and ate and pastured. And after that I saw the large and the black cattle, and behold all of them changed their stalls and pastures and their cattle, and began to live with each other' — Adam introduced as a WHITE BULL. The Animal Apocalypse's foundational allegorical code: humans-as-bovines, with colour-coding for righteousness (white = righteous; black = wicked; red = mixed). Tewahedo allegorical exegesis preserves the Adamic-white-bull image as the iconographic anchor for the eschatological reunification at 90:37-38.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 85:3, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And, behold, a calf was born of that white bull, and with it were born other calves, one of them white and the other black. And that first calf smote the white one and pursued him, and I saw till that white calf disappeared' — Cain (black) kills Abel (white). The allegorical structure sets up the dual-line genealogy that runs through the entire Animal Apocalypse: a white line (righteous Sethite-Noachic-Abrahamic descent) and a black line (Cainite wickedness). Tewahedo homilies on Cain/Abel preserve this colour-coded allegorical structure.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 85:4, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And again I saw with mine eyes as I slept, and I saw the heaven above, and behold a star fell from heaven, and it arose and ate and pastured amongst those oxen. And after that I saw the large and the black cattle' — the first star to fall in the Animal Apocalypse identifies as Asael / Azazel (the same figure judged in 1En 10:13). The allegorical concentration here recasts the entire Watchers narrative in animal-form as preface to the human historical narrative.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 86:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And again I saw in the vision, and looked towards the heaven, and behold I saw many stars descend and cast themselves down from heaven to that first star, and they became bulls amongst those cattle and pastured with them amongst them' — the 200 watchers fall as stars. Tewahedo angelic-history teaching uses 86:3 with 1En 6:5-7 (also pinned in γ.4.4.B) as the two complementary witnesses to the same event: the Watchers narrative IS the cosmological precondition for human history.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 86:3, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And I raised mine eyes again to heaven, and I saw in the vision, and behold there came forth from heaven beings who were like white men: and four went forth from that place and three with them' — the four white men are the four archangels of presence (Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, Phanuel — matching 1En 40:2-9 pinned in γ.4.4.C). The seven-archangel ecclesiology that Tewahedo preserves uniquely uses this Animal-Apocalypse vision as one of its three witnesses (with 9:1 and 20:1).
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 87:2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And those three that had last come forth grasped me by my hand and took me up, away from the generations of the earth, and raised me up to a lofty place, and showed me a tower raised high above the earth' — Enoch translated by three archangels to view world history from above. Tewahedo monastic-mystical tradition uses this verse as a canonical example of the contemplative ascent that the highest stages of monastic prayer approximate.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 87:3, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And I saw one of those four who had come forth first, and he seized that first star which had fallen from the heaven, and bound it hand and foot and cast it into an abyss: now that abyss was narrow and deep, and horrible and dark' — Asael's binding by Michael (parallel to 10:4-6). Tewahedo demonology reads the binding-of-Azazel as a TEMPORAL binding in the cosmic narrative that culminates in the eschatological judgment at 90:24 — providing the two-stage pattern that Rev 20:1-10 follows.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 88:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And one of them drew his sword, and gave it to those elephants and camels and asses: then they began to smite each other, and the whole earth quaked because of them. And as I was beholding in the vision, lo, one of those four who had come forth, hurled (a book) from heaven, and gathered and took all the great stars whose privy members were like those of horses, and bound them all hand and foot, and cast them into an abyss of the earth' — all 200 watchers bound. The full Watchers-judgment scene preserved in the Animal Apocalypse as one of its inaugurating actions, before human history proper begins.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 88:3, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And one of those four went to that white bull and instructed him in a secret, without his being terrified: he was born a bull and became a man, and built for himself a great vessel and dwelt thereon; and three bulls dwelt with him in that vessel' — Noah translated from BULL to MAN (rare ontological-elevation in the allegory). The transformation is theologically loaded: a righteous human in the Animal Apocalypse can be REMADE-into-something-higher. Tewahedo deification theology cites this as the canonical precedent (with Enoch's transfiguration at 71:11) for the doctrine of theosis as ontological-not-merely-moral transformation.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 89:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And those three that came forth, and all the (four) cattle came with them: and amongst them was a white bull and a red, like a wild ass' — Noah's three sons as bulls (Shem white, Ham black, Japheth red — the common Tewahedo identification matching the table of nations of Gen 10). Tewahedo genealogical tradition preserves the Hamitic identification of Ethiopia (descent from Cush son of Ham) but reads it WITHOUT the curse-of-Ham racialisation that Western Christianity often imposed: in Tewahedo reading, the colour-coding in 89:9 is allegorical, not ethnic.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 89:9, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And those (cattle) began to be born among them and to multiply: and they were divided amongst themselves into species' — the table-of-nations moment. Tewahedo ethnogenesis-teaching (preserved in the Kebra Nagast and in monastic genealogical chronicles) traces all peoples to legitimate divine ordering — the multiplication-and-division of peoples is positive, not curse-driven, anchoring an anti-supremacist Tewahedo theological anthropology.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 89:10, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the white bull begat a wild ass, and a white bull with it: and the wild ass multiplied. But that bull which was born from him begat a black wild boar and a white sheep' — Abraham (white bull) begets Ishmael (wild ass) and Isaac (white bull); Isaac then begets Esau (black wild boar) and Jacob (white sheep). The sheep-as-Israel allegory begins here. Tewahedo ecclesiology preserves the sheep-of-the-flock identification through the Anaphora of the Apostles (where 'sheep of Thy pasture' resonates with this Animal-Apocalypse imagery).
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 89:12, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the descendants of that white bull begat twelve sheep, and those twelve sheep were given over into the hand of dogs' — the twelve sons of Jacob given over to oppressors (sold-into-Egypt allegory) but already preserving the sheep-as-the-twelve-tribes identification. Tewahedo reading of Israel-Egypt history through this Enochic allegorical lens preserves a distinctive emphasis: the sheep-shape of God's people is eternal; the form persists through every oppression.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 89:14, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And those sheep ascended and came to a house, and the Lord of the sheep stood upon it. And all the sheep prostrated themselves before Him: I saw all the sheep gathered together and bowing down before the throne' — Sinai theophany: the wilderness tabernacle as 'house' for the sheep. Tewahedo tabot-theology (the tablets-in-the-ark as the abiding presence) draws on 89:36 as scriptural anchor: the house-of-the-sheep is where the Lord-of-the-sheep dwells, transferring from wilderness tabernacle to Tewahedo qǝddǝst-qǝddusan (holy of holies) by continuous succession.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 89:36, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the dogs began to rend, and the foxes to devour, and the wild boars to eat the sheep, until the Lord of the sheep raised up a ram from amongst them, who led them' — gentile oppressors as dogs (Philistines), foxes (Ammonites), wild boars (Edomites/Amalekites); the ram raised up is Samuel (or Saul). Tewahedo homiletics on the Judges-Samuel narrative preserves the allegorical-spiritual reading alongside the historical: every oppression is also a spiritual war.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 89:42, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the sheep increased and multiplied: and all those dogs, and foxes, and wild boars feared and fled before them, and that ram pushed and killed the wild beasts: and they had no more power amongst the sheep, and robbed them no more of ought. And that house became great and broad, and a high tower was built upon the house' — David / Solomon era: the house grows great, the tower (TEMPLE) is built upon it. Tewahedo ecclesiology preserves the tower-on-house imagery (church-on-Christ-the-rock, with the temple as eschatological prefiguration of the Tewahedo qǝddǝst) as the canonical anticipation of the ecclesial structure.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 89:50, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And He gave them over into the hands of the lions and tigers, and wolves and hyenas, and into the hand of the foxes, and to all the wild beasts: and those wild beasts began to tear those sheep in pieces. And He forsook the house of their fathers, and their tower, and gave them all into the hand of the lions, to tear and devour them' — the Babylonian exile: the tower is forsaken, the sheep given to lions (Babylon). Tewahedo exilic-theology preserves the lesson: when the house-of-the-Lord becomes empty, God's people are scattered. The Tewahedo preservation of Solomon's-temple-tradition through the ark-narrative is read as the providential antidote.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 89:55, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And He called seventy shepherds, and cast those sheep to them that they might pasture them, and He spake to the shepherds and their companions: Let each individual of you pasture the sheep henceforward, and everything that I shall command you that do ye' — the seventy shepherds period (from exile to eschaton, the period of gentile dominion). Tewahedo reading interprets the seventy as covering the entire intertestamental and Greco-Roman period: the time when God's people are RULED by foreign shepherds. The 70 cycle echoes Jer 25:11-12 / Dan 9:24-27 but spans a longer epoch.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 89:59, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'But behold lambs were borne by those white sheep, and they began to open their eyes and to see, and to cry to the sheep' — the awakening of the lambs (the Hasidic/early-Maccabean reformist movement, the small remnant who saw the apostasy and cried out). Tewahedo monastic-reform history (the multiple movements of monastic renewal in Ethiopian church history) draws typological parallels to 90:6: the small remnant that opens its eyes is the canonical pattern of every spiritual renewal.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 90:6, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And I saw till that man, who wrote down the names of the shepherds and carried them up before the Lord of the sheep, came and helped that ram and showed him everything: his help came down' — the angelic scribe-intercessor helps the Maccabean leader. Tewahedo angelic-mediation theology preserves this image of the heavenly-scribe-who-records-and-intervenes (essentially identical to the role given Michael/Phanuel in other Enochic strata).
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 90:14, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And I saw till a throne was erected in the pleasant land, and the Lord of the sheep sat Himself thereon, and the other took the sealed books and opened those books before the Lord of the sheep' — the eschatological throne of judgment with the books opened. Direct verbal preparation for Dan 7:9-10 and Rev 20:11-12; the Tewahedo eschatological-judgment iconography preserves the books-before-the-throne as load-bearing in Mäṣḥafä Berhan (Book of Light) tradition.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 90:20, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the judgment was held first over the stars, and they were judged and found guilty, and went to the place of condemnation, and they were cast into an abyss, full of fire and flaming, and full of pillars of fire' — final judgment of the fallen watchers (the long-anticipated eschatological reckoning, complementing their preliminary binding at 10:4-6 and 88:1-3). Tewahedo demonology reads the two-stage pattern (binding now, fire-judgment at eschaton) as the canonical model: evil is RESTRAINED but not yet FINALLY DESTROYED in the present age.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 90:24, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And I stood up to see till they folded up that old house; and carried off all the pillars, and all the beams and ornaments of the house were at the same time folded up with it, and they carried it off and laid it in a place in the south of the land. And I saw till the Lord of the sheep brought a new house greater and loftier than that first, and set it up in the place of the first which had been folded up: all its pillars were new, the columns new; and the ornaments new and larger than those of the first, the old one which He had taken away, and all the sheep were within it' — the new Jerusalem / new house replacing the old. Tewahedo eschatology reads this verse as direct anticipation of Rev 21:2-3 (new Jerusalem descending), with the Tewahedo distinctive emphasis that the new house is GREATER than the first — escalation, not mere restoration.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 90:28, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And all that had been destroyed and dispersed, and all the beasts of the field, and all the birds of the heaven, assembled in that house, and the Lord of the sheep rejoiced with great joy because they were all good and had returned to His house' — the eschatological conversion of the Gentiles (the beasts and birds — all non-Israel peoples — gathered into the house). Tewahedo missiological theology takes 90:30 as the canonical anticipation of catholic-as-universal (the gathering of the nations into the one house). The verse undergirds the Tewahedo self-understanding as ALREADY-being-part-of-this-gathering by virtue of the Ethiopian eunuch's baptism (Acts 8:26-39).
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 90:30, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And I saw till all their generations were transformed, and they all became white bulls; and the first among them became a lamb, and that lamb became a great animal and had great black horns on its head; and the Lord of the sheep rejoiced over it and over all the bulls' — final reunification: ALL become white bulls again (return to the Adamic state). The lamb-with-great-black-horns is the eschatological messianic figure (distinct from the white-bull-with-great-horns at 90:37, which represents the Davidic-messianic line). Tewahedo Christology reads the two figures together: 90:37 (Christ as new Adam — white bull) plus 90:38 (Christ as Lamb-of-God with horns of authority) presents both Christological registers in a single Animal-Apocalypse climax.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 90:38, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And after that Enoch began to speak from the books, and he said: Concerning the children of righteousness and concerning the elect of the world, and concerning the plant of uprightness, I will speak these things, yea, I Enoch will declare them unto you, my sons: According to that which appeared to me in the heavenly vision, and which I have known through the word of the holy angels, and have learnt from the heavenly tablets' — Enoch reads the seven-weeks scheme from the heavenly tablets. Tewahedo historiographical tradition (preserved in monastic chronicles like the Mäṣḥafä Sǝnksar) follows the principle that history is READABLE: cosmic order is given in advance and the inspired reader can perceive its pattern.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 93:2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And after that in the second week great wickedness shall arise, and deceit shall have sprung up; and in it there shall be the first end. And in it a man shall be saved' — second week: the Flood and Noah's preservation. The Apocalypse of Weeks compresses the entire Watchers + Flood narrative into a single 'week' phrase. Tewahedo periodisation tradition preserves this compression-friendly approach to biblical history: the meaningful units are EPOCHS, not individual events.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 93:5, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And after that in the third week at its close a man shall be elected as the plant of righteous judgement, and his posterity shall become the plant of righteousness for evermore' — third week: Abraham elected as the 'plant of righteousness'. Tewahedo covenant theology preserves the plant-of-righteousness image (parallel to Jer 23:5, Isa 11:1 'shoot from stump of Jesse') as the textual basis for the Davidic-messianic line rooted in Abrahamic election: the plant Abraham becomes the plant Israel becomes the plant Christ.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 93:6, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And after that in the fifth week, at its close, the house of glory and dominion shall be built for ever' — fifth week: Solomon's temple. Tewahedo temple-theology preserves the 'house of glory and dominion' language as anticipating both the qǝddǝst-qǝddusan (Tewahedo holy of holies) and the eschatological new house of 1En 90:28-29. Solomon's temple is read as historical prefiguration, not termination, of God's dwelling-among-his-people.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 93:8, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And after that in the sixth week all who live in it shall be blinded, and the hearts of all of them shall godlessly forsake wisdom. And in it a man shall ascend; and at its close the house of dominion shall be burnt with fire, and the whole race of the chosen root shall be dispersed' — sixth week: the period of the prophets, Elijah's ascension, and the destruction of Solomon's temple (586 BCE). Tewahedo prophetic tradition reads the 'man shall ascend' as Elijah's translation (cf. 2 Kgs 2:11) — Elijah and Enoch as the two pre-Christian witnesses to bodily translation into heaven.
